title: Post-filtering
summary: Retrieve the top candidates first, then drop the ones the caller may not read. It is simple, and it fails when most candidates are denied.
useIf: Nearly every document is visible to nearly every caller, or the index cannot filter on permissions.
avoidIf: Access is selective: a caller sees a few percent of the corpus, or denied text must never leave the index.

explain.md: A post-filter runs **after** ranking. The app asks the index for the top candidates, checks each against an ACL source and keeps the allowed ones. The problem is arithmetic. If the caller may read a fraction *f* of the corpus, a top-k list holds about k times *f* allowed documents, and relevance does not care about permissions.

explain.title: Over-fetch for a post-filter

vars.v: visible fraction: the share of the corpus the caller may read

explain.example: For 10 results, f = 50% needs 20 candidates, f = 10% needs 100 and f = 2% needs 500. This is the lab's model, which assumes relevance is independent of permission: the *ACL decision space* lab shows the group-based case (f = 5%, k = 10, 3x over-fetch) returning a median of 1 result with about 22% empty answers.

explain.md: Large over-fetch costs rerank and latency, so **filter immediately after retrieval, before the reranker, logs and caches**. Denied text that reaches those stages is a leak surface even if the user never sees it. That is the main reason a post-filter fails an audit for regulated content.

explain.title: Your pre-filter may be a post-filter
explain.md: In Azure AI Search, `vectorFilterMode` has three values: `preFilter`, `postFilter` and `strictPostFilter` (preview). New indexes default to `preFilter`, but indexes created before about 2023-10-15 default to `postFilter`, which can miss results for selective filters. `strictPostFilter` finds the global top k first and has the highest risk of false negatives [[tr19]].

whereToUse: Prototypes and small corpora where nearly all content is public to the audience
A search service that cannot be changed to hold ACL fields
A second check after a pre-filter, using the live source for the top few hits
Wikis and handbooks where only a minority of pages are restricted

use: You cannot add ACL fields to the index
A permission lookup per candidate is cheap and fast
avoid: Access is selective and top-k must stay full
Denied text must not reach rerankers, logs or caches
Each caller sees a tiny slice of a large corpus
flips: The visible fraction falls below about 10%: move the filter into the index
A regulator or contract forbids denied text outside the index: pre-filter or isolate
A reranker is expensive: filter first or the over-fetch bill grows

pitfalls.symptom: Some users get one result or none
pitfalls.cause: Over-fetch is fixed while their visible fraction is small
pitfalls.fix: Compute k_fetch from the caller's visible fraction, cap it, and fall back to a pre-filter

pitfalls.symptom: Restricted text appears in logs and traces
pitfalls.cause: Candidates were logged before the filter ran
pitfalls.fix: Filter first, then log ids and decisions only

pitfalls.symptom: Recall drops although the code never filters in the index
pitfalls.cause: The index defaults to postFilter for vector queries
pitfalls.fix: Set vectorFilterMode explicitly and recreate old indexes to use preFilter

scenarios.title: Five percent visible, top ten required
scenarios.situation: An assistant over 2 million chunks needs ten results per query. Callers belong to team groups and see about 5% of the corpus. The search service can filter on a filterable field. The p95 budget is 800 ms.
unknowns: Can ACL fields be added at ingest?
How often do group memberships change?
scenarios.question: Where do you filter?

options.name: Keep the post-filter and fetch 10
options.why: About half a result survives on average, and many queries return nothing.
options.tradeoff: Only works when nearly everything is visible.

options.name: Post-filter with over-fetch of 200 and an early filter
options.tradeoff: Ten times the fetch, more reranker load and denied text in your code.

options.name: Move the permission filter into the index as a security filter
options.why: Ranking sees only allowed chunks, so top-k stays full [[r13]].
options.tradeoff: Needs ACL capture at ingest, a sync story and a recall check under selective filters.

flips.then: A post-filter with small over-fetch is simpler and fine.

flips.if: ACL fields cannot be added to the index
flips.then: Over-fetch and early filtering is the only option, so cap the cost.

scenarios.takeaway: At low visible fractions the filter belongs inside the index.

scenarios.title: Auditors forbid denied text outside the index
scenarios.situation: A legal-hold corpus is queried by case teams. Auditors require that restricted text never reaches application logs, rerankers or caches unless the caller may read it. Visibility varies widely.
constraints: Denied text must stay in the index
unknowns: Which stages log candidate text today?
Can ACLs be copied into the index?
scenarios.question: Which approach passes the audit?

options.name: Pre-filter in the index and log only ids and decisions
options.why: Denied text never leaves the engine, and the logs hold no restricted content.
options.tradeoff: ACL sync lag must be stated and tested.

options.name: Post-filter with a very large over-fetch
options.why: Over-fetch does not change who sees denied text: your code, reranker and logs still do.
options.tradeoff: Fine for public content where denied text is not sensitive.

options.name: Post-filter inside a hardened service that never logs candidates
options.why: Contains the exposure to one trusted component.
options.tradeoff: You must prove the isolation and still waste top-k.

flips.then: The hardened post-filter service is the fallback.
Apply the strict path to those matters only.

scenarios.takeaway: Ask which stage sees denied text, and not only whether the user sees it.

scenarios.title: Recall drops on an older index
scenarios.situation: A team reports poor recall for restricted callers on a vector index created in 2022. Their filter is a security filter and queries use the default settings.
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.name: Switch to strictPostFilter
options.why: It finds the global top k first and has the highest risk of false negatives for selective filters [[tr19]].
options.tradeoff: It is a preview mode and suits cases where global ranking matters more than recall.

options.name: Recreate the index and set vectorFilterMode to preFilter explicitly
options.why: Older indexes default to postFilter and need to be recreated to use preFilter [[tr19]].

options.name: Raise k to compensate
options.tradeoff: More candidates per query and still lossy at small visible fractions.

flips.if: Recreating the index is not possible this quarter
flips.then: Raise k as a stopgap and track recall for restricted callers.

flips.if: The index is newer than October 2023
flips.then: preFilter is already the default. Look at sync and ACL data instead.

scenarios.takeaway: Check which filter mode your engine really uses.

quiz.q: A caller may read 4% of the corpus. You need 10 results after a post-filter. About how many candidates must you fetch?
quiz.explain: 10 divided by 0.04 is 250. This assumes relevance is independent of permission, so real numbers vary. It shows why post-filtering gets expensive as f shrinks.

quiz.q: You must keep a post-filter for now. Where should it run?
options: After the reranker, so only the final list is checked
At the client, after the answer streams
Immediately after retrieval, before the reranker, logs and caches
After the model generates the answer
quiz.explain: Filtering first keeps denied text away from rerankers, logs and caches. Later stages already saw it, and a model cannot be trusted to omit what it saw.

flashcards.front: What is the over-fetch formula for a post-filter?
flashcards.back: k_fetch = ceil(k_needed / f), where f is the visible fraction. At f = 2% and 10 wanted results, fetch 500. It assumes relevance is independent of permission.

flashcards.front: What does a post-filter expose that a pre-filter does not?
flashcards.back: Denied text reaches your code, rerankers, logs and caches before it is dropped. A pre-filter keeps it inside the index.

flashcards.front: Which Azure AI Search vector filter mode is the default for newer indexes?
flashcards.back: preFilter. Indexes created before about 2023-10-15 default to postFilter and must be recreated to use preFilter.
